newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algerians start voting for multi-party parliament.
newsitem.headline: Algerians start voting for multi-party parliament.

text.p: Algerians started voting on Thursday in the first parliamentary election in more than five years of violence and bloodshed -- blamed by officials on Moslem fundamentalists.

Armed plainclothes police guarded polling stations, most of which opened at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT). Heavily armed troops and police, backed by armoured troop carriers, deployed in sunny, warm weather at entrances to Algiers and in city streets where Moslem rebels have carried out attacks.

"I voted for peace for me and my children," Ahmed Yanaguen, 58, told Reuters. Yanaguen and his wife, wearing a black veil, were the first to vote at El-Warda school in the capital's Telemly neighbourhood.
The deputy head of the El-Warda station said voting was slow but expected it to pick up in the next few hours.
Voters are casting ballots to elect a 380-member National Assembly (lower house) from more than 7,000 candidates representing 39 political parties.
Officials at some poll stations said last-minute organisation hitches forced them to delay opening by up to an hour.

The government of President Liamine Zeroual says the poll is a key step towards ending civil strife that began shortly after the army-backed authorities in January 1992 cancelled elections that radical Islamists were poised to win.
About 60,000 people have died in the conflict.
In three days upto last Monday, a series of bomb attacks by suspected Moslem rebels in the capital killed 22 people and wounded about 120.
More than 37,500 polling stations will remain open until 7 p.m. (1800 GMT) although local authorities may extend polling hours in some centres to help voters.

The new parliament will be Algeria's first elected multi-party assembly since independence in 1962. For nearly three decades until the first attempt at a democratic parliamentary vote in December 1991, the oil and gas producing country was run as a one-party state by the National Liberation Front (FLN).

The frontrunners at the elections are the National Democratic Rally (RND), which groups Zeroual supporters, and the Islam-oriented Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) of moderate Islamist leader Mahfoud Nahnah.
Other leading parties include the Socialist Forces Front (FFS) of secularist opposition leader Hocine Ait Ahmed and the Rally for Culture and Democracy of anti-Islamist Said Saadi.
A new proportional representation law virtually guarantees that at least four or five parties will be in parliament with little chance of a single party holding an absolute majority.
Because of the new system, officials are reluctant to forecast when final results will be available. Newspapers say they should be out some time on Friday.
Nearly 200 officials from the United Nations, Organisation of African Unity and the Arab League are monitoring the voting.
Algerian newspaper on Thursday again printed an Interior Ministry statement urging civilians to report all suspicious vehicles or packages at bus stops and crowded streets.

The authorities this week ordered all weekly markets and some schools to close until after the election. An old ban on parking cars in crowded streets was also reinforced in a further effort to thwart bomb attacks.
